CausalChain: Chronic liver injury → Increased ECM deposition and matrix stiffness → Activation of integrin–FAK–MEK/ERK signaling in tissue‐resident Kupffer cells → Polarization into M2-like TAMs → Secretion of IL-10, TGF-β, and promotion of angiogenesis/EMT → Tumor progression and immunosuppression.
Hypothesis: Modulating the mechanical properties of the liver tumor microenvironment to decrease matrix stiffness will reprogram M2-polarized TAMs toward a proinflammatory M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing antitumor immune responses and improving the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Here, we propose that the mechanical characteristics of the liver tumor microenvironment, particularly matrix stiffness, play a central role in dictating the polarization state of resident macrophages. The altered extracellular matrix resulting from chronic liver injury enhances tumor stiffness, which in turn activates integrin‐mediated signaling pathways in Kupffer cells, driving their maturation into M2‐polarized tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). These M2 TAMs secrete immunosuppressive cytokines and angiogenic factors, thus contributing to tumor progression and resistance to checkpoint inhibitors. We hypothesize that by modulating matrix stiffness, it may be possible to reprogram these M2 TAMs toward an M1 phenotype, thereby restoring effective anticancer immunity and sensitizing hepatocellular carcinoma to current immunotherapy strategies.
